newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein barred again as N.Irish talks resume.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein barred again as N.Irish talks resume.

text.p: Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, was again locked out of talks on the future of Northern Ireland on Tuesday as attempts resumed to nurse the ailing peace process back to life.
As leaders of the main political parties gathered to resume talks adjourned during Britain's May national election campaign, a Sinn Fein delegation was met with padlocked gates.
"Is there any possibility of even opening this gate so that we can have a civilised conversation?" Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams asked officials outside a government centre in Belfast.
"I'm afraid not," said an official without emotion.
Mo Mowlam, Northern Ireland Secretary in Britain's newly-elected Labour government, had earlier ruled out a talks seat for Sinn Fein while its Irish Republican Army ally was on a war footing.
"We would prefer to have Sinn Fein around the table rather than not but that is dependent on a meaningful ceasefire, an unequivocal ceasefire with supporting words and deeds," Mowlam told BBC radio.
Britain, backed by Ireland, says no party at the table can have a private army lurking in the background.

The talks, which first started a year ago, were adjourned during British elections, which returned a Labour government after 18 years of Conservative rule and raised hopes of a breakthrough in the bitter conflict over British rule of Northern Ireland.

Talks chairman George Mitchell, a former U.S. senator, expressed optimism over the new round despite an upsurge of guerrilla activity by both Republican and pro-British Loyalist extremists in the past few days.

"We believe that an opportunity exists to move forward in the process and we hope very much that there will be substantive progress in these talks in the near future," Mitchell told reporters as the talks got under way.
"I think it is a fair statement...that progress in the past year has been little and has been slow and we hope that there will be more of it and faster now that we have returned," he said.
Adams, reading a protest statement calling for Sinn Fein's admission to the talks, said the talks were vital to finding a political solution to Northern Ireland.
"Locking Sinn Fein out of these talks can be no part of that," he said.

A six week lull in IRA activity ended over the weekend in a 500 kg (1,100 pound) bomb scare in Belfast. Police found the explosives, which did not go off, in a burnt-out van and said the IRA had tried to lure them into a trap.

Pro-British Protestant hardliners, in the runup to what is feared will be a turbulent period of parades through Catholic zones, were blamed on Sunday for the mob killing of a police officer, who was kicked to death.
"Loyalist" militias, pledged to thwart the IRA's aim of ending British rule, have shot dead two Catholic nationalists in the past year and injured others in booby-trap bomb attacks.
Tuesday's talks start with a short round-table session and then return to a pattern of bilateral discussions between the Protestant and Catholic parties and the British and Irish governments.
Overshadowed by resurgent guerrilla activity, the talks struggled to make any progress during their first year.

Politicians spent the early months arguing over procedures and were then embroiled in unresolved disputes over the terms for Sinn Fein's entry and how to achieve disarmament by the rival guerrilla groups.
Mitchell suggested on Tuesday that he might bring forward his own initiative in a bid to get round the disarmament issue but declined to give details.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said he was approaching the talks with "hope and optimism".

"The reality of Sinn Fein is that they have the key in their own pocket. They have the key to that gate. We want a restoration of the ceasefire and once that is done we will obviously try to get them into talks," Spring told reporters.
